*Computed ranges are reconstructions that depend on the named chronology model and the stated assumptions. They are not independent dates.*


**Chronological statements:**

- “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon” (Daniel 7:1) → `before` Belshazzar slain; Darius the Mede receives the kingdom (Dan 5:30–31); assumptions: Belshazzar's "first year" precedes his death (Dan 5:30). No other model-independent date is assigned.
- “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon” (Daniel 7:1) → `years_later` reign of Belshazzar (Belshazzar's years counted from the entrusting of the kingship); assumptions: Only in the regency model: "first year" is counted from the entrusting of the kingship.; Offset 0–1 years (window up to two years from the start) covers both counting the first twelve months and an accession-year count; the convention Daniel used is unknown. [1, 3]

## Competing reconstructions

- **Undated (model-independent)** (This project's default): Without a Babylonian count of Belshazzar's years the vision is placed only before Belshazzar's death (Oct 539). [4]
- **Counted from the entrusting of the kingship (c. 553 BC)** (R. P. Dougherty (1929) on the regency's start; counting basis assumed here): If Daniel counts from Nabonidus's delegation of kingship, the first year falls c. 553–551 BC. Shown only in the "Belshazzar's years" model. [1, 3, 2]
- **Composition in the Maccabean crisis** (S. R. Driver (1900), J. J. Collins (1984), via Wikipedia): The vision was written c. 167–164 BC, before the Temple's rededication; the date formula is literary. [5, 6]
- **Composition in the 6th century BC** (Jerome, R. D. Wilson (1917), D. Guzik): The vision was seen and written by Daniel in Belshazzar's reign, as stated. [7, 8, 9]

## Claims and evidence

### Nabonidus entrusted the kingship in Babylonia to Belshazzar around the start of his third year (c. 553 BC).

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

The Verse Account says so directly ("when the third year was about to begin"); the Chronicle places the western campaign in year 3 and the king in Tayma, with the prince in Akkad, in years 7–11; Smith's correlation is reported by Dougherty.

- *Supporting (direct):* "When the third year was about to begin" Nabonidus entrusted the army to his eldest son and "entrusted the kingship to him". (col. ii 5–6 (Livius numbering)) [1]
- *Supporting (direct):* Year 3: campaign to Amurru and Edom (Abu–Kislimu); years 7–11: the king in Tayma, the prince in Akkad. (i 11–17 (year 3); ii 5 ff. (years 7, 9–11)) [2]
- *Context (indirect):* Smith showed the Verse Account's Tema campaign accords with the Chronicle's 3rd year; Dougherty treats Belshazzar as co-regent from then. (pp. 105–107) [3]

*Limitations:* The Verse Account is hostile polemic; the Chronicle's years 4–5 are lost. Beaulieu (1989) not read.

### Daniel's "first year of Belshazzar" can be fixed to a calendar year.

**Classification:** No independent corroboration found (machine proposed) · layer: reconstruction

No Babylonian text dates by Belshazzar's years. A date (c. 553–551 BC) follows only if Daniel counted from the entrusting of the kingship; that assumption is modelled separately and the event is otherwise left undated.

- *Context (direct):* "When the third year was about to begin" Nabonidus entrusted the army to his eldest son and "entrusted the kingship to him". (col. ii 5–6 (Livius numbering)) [1]
- *Context (direct):* Nabonidus year 2 began 19 Apr 554, year 3 on 7 Apr 553, year 4 on 26 Apr 552; no Belshazzar years appear in the dated documents. (Year tables (Nabonidus)) [4]

### Daniel saw this vision and wrote it down in Belshazzar's first year.

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: text

Traditional interpreters accept the date formula; critical scholars date the chapter to the Antiochene crisis (c. 167–164 BC) because its horizon ends with the little horn. The disagreement concerns authorship and date of composition and is unresolved.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Jerome treats the vision as seen in Belshazzar's first year and defends the book's prophetic authorship against Porphyry. (on 7:1; prologue) [7]
- *Challenging (indirect):* The age of Antiochus Epiphanes is "the limiting horizon of the book"; the visions culminate in his persecution. (pp. 98–100) [5]
- *Context (indirect):* Reports the critical dating of the visions to 167–164 BC, with ch. 7 somewhat earlier. (Composition (Collins 1984)) [6]

*Limitations:* Collins known here only via Wikipedia.

### Antiochus IV reigned over the Seleucid empire from Ulûlu 137 SE (175 BC) to Kislîmu 148 SE (late 164 BC).

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

The Babylonian King List gives his accession and death report; 1 Maccabees gives the same accession year and his death in 149 (Macedonian-reckoned era).

- *Supporting (direct):* Antiochus ascended in Ulûlu of year 137; in Kislîmu of year 148 "it was heard that" he had died. (rev. 9–14) [10]
- *Supporting (direct):* Reign from year 137; altar desecrated 15 Chislev 145; rededicated 25 Chislev 148; died in 149. (1 Macc 1:10, 54; 4:52–54; 6:16) [11]

*Limitations:* King List translation flagged for revision by its editor.

### Antiochus IV suppressed Temple worship in Jerusalem for about three years (Chislev 145 – Chislev 148 SE).

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

1 Maccabees, independent of Daniel, dates the "abomination of desolation" to 15 Chislev 145 and the rededication to 25 Chislev 148, with persecuting decrees before the desecration. It is a single (Jewish) source tradition in this session: non-Jewish confirmation (Diodorus 34/35) could not be accessed, and Polybius attests only Antiochus's notoriety.

- *Supporting (direct):* Reign from year 137; altar desecrated 15 Chislev 145; rededicated 25 Chislev 148; died in 149. (1 Macc 1:10, 54; 4:52–54; 6:16) [11]
- *Context (indirect):* His conduct earned him the nickname Epimanes, "madman". (26.1–1a) [12]

*Limitations:* One source tradition read (1 Maccabees); 2 Maccabees and Diodorus not read.

### Interpreters before the Christian era read the "one like a son of man" as an individual figure.

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

The Parables of Enoch present "that Son of Man" as an individual beside the Head of Days; Charles dates them c. 105–64 BC, but other scholars date them later, possibly after the start of the Christian era.

- *Supporting (direct):* Enoch sees one with "a head of days" and "that Son of Man" who has righteousness and will raise kings from their seats. (1 Enoch 46:1–4) [13]

*Limitations:* Dating of the Parables disputed (Driver reports Dillmann, Charles, Schürer).

## Related passages and events

- pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 → **proposed fulfillment** → Neo-Babylonian Empire (high): First beast = Babylon, by parallel with Dan 2:38 (head of gold = Nebuchadnezzar); accepted by every interpreter consulted. Not stated in Dan 7. [7, 5, 9]
- pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 → **proposed fulfillment** → Median kingdom (Media) (medium): Second beast = Media in the Grecian scheme. [5]
- pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 → **proposed fulfillment** → Achaemenid Persian Empire (medium): Second beast (Medo-Persia, Roman scheme) or third beast (Persia, Grecian scheme). [7, 5]
- pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 → **proposed fulfillment** → Macedonian empire of Alexander the Great (medium): Third beast (Roman scheme) or fourth beast with its successors (Grecian scheme; Porphyry). [7, 5]
- pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 → **proposed fulfillment** → Rome (Republic and Empire) (medium): Fourth beast = Rome in the traditional scheme (2 Esdras 12:11 onward). [11, 7, 14]
- pro_01M4TSKK93WKW4EN8EJXKHK5P6 → **proposed fulfillment** → Antiochus IV Epiphanes (medium): Little horn = Antiochus IV in the Grecian scheme, matching the little horn of ch. 8. [7, 5]
- pro_01M4TSKK93WKW4EN8EJXKHK5P6 → **proposed fulfillment** → Seleucid empire (medium): Ten horns = Seleucid kings (several reconstructions). [5]
- pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 → **thematic parallel** → pro_01M4RTK7458JMN36GV9R7JAAMQ (high): Four kingdoms followed by God's everlasting kingdom, as in the statue dream; "generally agreed" to be the same four (Driver p. 94). [5, 7]
- Mark 14:62 → **direct reference** → pro_01M4TSKK93MG64C8YGN1J0YB11 (high): "You will see the Son of Man … coming with the clouds of the sky" (cf. Matt 26:64).
- Matthew 24:30 → **direct reference** → pro_01M4TSKK93MG64C8YGN1J0YB11 (high): The Son of Man coming on the clouds (cf. Mark 13:26).
- Revelation 1:13–14 → **direct reference** → vis_01M4TSKK93X3TER65WRMC8FYYV (high): "One like a son of man" with hair "white as white wool, like snow" — combining the son of man and the Ancient of Days.
- Revelation 13:1–7 → **direct reference** → vis_01M4TSKK93X3TER65WRMC8FYYV (high): A beast from the sea with ten horns, leopard/bear/lion features, a mouth speaking great things, 42 months, war on the saints.
- Revelation 12:14 → **direct reference** → pro_01M4TSKK93WKW4EN8EJXKHK5P6 (high): "A time, times, and half a time."
- pro_01M4TSKK93WKW4EN8EJXKHK5P6 → **thematic parallel** → Daniel 12:7 (high): The same period, "a time, times, and a half".
- pro_01M4TSKK93WKW4EN8EJXKHK5P6 → **thematic parallel** → Daniel 8:9–12 (medium): The little horn of ch. 8; whether it is the same figure is the crux between the schemes (Driver; Newton). [5, 14]
- 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) → **direct reference** → pro_01M4TSKK93XSNXYTSP754Z4VR2 (high): 2 Esdras 12:11–12: the eagle (Rome) "is the fourth kingdom which appeared in a vision to your brother Daniel". [11]
- pro_01M4TSKK93MG64C8YGN1J0YB11 → **thematic parallel** → 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) (high): 2 Esdras 13:1–3: a man from the sea who "flew with the clouds of heaven". [11]
- pro_01M4TSKK93MG64C8YGN1J0YB11 → **thematic parallel** → 1 Enoch, Book of Parables (Similitudes), chs. 37–71 (high): The Head of Days and the Son of Man (1 Enoch 46) reuse Dan 7:9–13. [13, 5]
- Belshazzar slain; Darius the Mede receives the kingdom (Dan 5:30–31) → **preceded by** → this event (high): The vision is dated to Belshazzar's first year, before his death (5:30); Jerome notes chs. 7–8 are "historically prior" to chs. 5–6. [7]
- this event → **thematic parallel** → Nebuchadnezzar's dream and Daniel's interpretation (Dan 2:1–45) (high): Parallel revelation of four kingdoms and God's kingdom.

## Commentary (interpretation, not historical evidence)

- Guzik gives no BC date, placing the vision between chapters 4 and 5. He reads the four beasts as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, the ten horns and the little horn as still future (a coming Antichrist from a restored Roman order), the Ancient of Days as God the Father, and the son of man as Jesus; the "time, times and half a time" is the last three and a half years before Christ's return. [9]

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- Beaulieu (1989) on Nabonidus's departure not read.
- Collins (1993 Hermeneia; 1998) not read directly — angelic and composition views secondary.
- Old Greek and Qumran texts of Daniel 7 not consulted.
- Calvin's Daniel commentary not read directly.
- Diodorus 34/35.1 not accessible.
- Canaanite (Baal–Yamm/El) background claims seen only uncited in Wikipedia; not recorded.
- Read Beaulieu, The Reign of Nabonidus (1989), on the date of Nabonidus's departure.
- Old Greek Daniel 7 (notably its reading of 7:13) not read.
- Qumran manuscripts of Daniel 7 not consulted.
- Calvin's commentary (Julius Caesar view) not read directly.
- Diodorus 34/35.1 (Antiochus in the Temple) not accessible on LacusCurtius.

## Disputes

- Daniel saw this vision and wrote it down in Belshazzar's first year.

event.title: Daniel's vision of the ram and the goat at Susa (Dan 8)
event.summary: In the third year of Belshazzar Daniel sees, at Susa by the Ulai, a ram and a goat, four horns and a little horn that desolates the sanctuary; Gabriel explains it, and Daniel falls ill. This record is the narrated experience; symbols and interpretations are separate records.

claims.statement: Alexander of Macedon overthrew the Persian empire (Arbela, 331 BC; death of Darius III, 330 BC).
claims.reasoning: Arrian dates the decisive battle to the archonship of Aristophanes (331/330) and Darius's death to that of Aristophon (330/329). This is the historical background against which 8:5–7 and 8:21 are read; it is not itself an identification of the symbols.

claims.statement: After Alexander, four of his successors (Cassander, Lysimachus, Ptolemy, Seleucus) acted as kings in alliance against Antigonus.
claims.reasoning: Diodorus describes the four-king coalition before Ipsus. Jerome lists a different four, so the "four kingdoms" of 8:22 are matched to different sets by different interpreters.

claims.statement: Daniel was physically at Susa when he saw the vision.
claims.reasoning: Guzik reads 8:27 ("the king's business") as Daniel being in Shushan on official business; Driver reads 8:2 as describing where Daniel saw himself in the vision. In Belshazzar's time Susa lay outside Babylonian rule, which bears on the question but was not researched further.

claims.statement: Alexander was shown the Book of Daniel at Jerusalem.
claims.reasoning: Reported only by Josephus. Arrian's narrative of the campaign from Tyre to Gaza and Egypt does not mention Jerusalem.
limitations: Absence in Arrian is not disproof.

claims.statement: Gabriel explained the vision to Daniel.
claims.reasoning: An angelic revelation cannot be assessed historically. This is not a theological verdict.

# Daniel's vision of the ram and the goat at Susa (Dan 8)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 8:1–2 (superscription): Third year of Belshazzar; Susa, by the Ulai.
- Daniel 8:15–19 (narration)
- Daniel 8:27 (narration)

## Biblical account

In Belshazzar's third year Daniel sees himself at the citadel of Susa by the Ulai. A two-horned ram is overthrown by a swift goat whose great horn is broken and replaced by four; from one comes a little horn that attacks the host of heaven, removes the continual offering and casts down the sanctuary for 2,300 evenings and mornings. Gabriel explains that the ram is the kings of Media and Persia and the goat the king of Greece, and foretells a fierce king who will be broken without human hand. Daniel falls ill, then returns to the king's business.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Narrative setting: Belshazzar's regency (third year); composition date disputed (see Daniel 7)

Susa was the capital of Elam and later a principal residence of the Persian kings (Neh 1:1; Esth 1:2). In Belshazzar's time it lay outside Babylonian control. The Ulai was a stream or canal at Susa; its course is not precisely identified (Pleiades marks the candidate river with a question mark). [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Belshazzar: Regent ("king" in Daniel)

## Competing reconstructions

- **Daniel at Susa only "in the vision"** (S. R. Driver (1900)): 8:2 describes "where Daniel seemed to find himself in the vision". [1]
- **Daniel physically at Susa on royal business** (D. Guzik): He was in Shushan "on business for the king" (8:27). [5]
- **Dated by the regency count (c. 551–549 BC)** (This project's "Belshazzar's years" model): Two years after the vision of ch. 7 (Jerome: "two years after the previous revelation"). Undated outside that model. [1]

## Claims and evidence

### Alexander of Macedon overthrew the Persian empire (Arbela, 331 BC; death of Darius III, 330 BC).

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Arrian dates the decisive battle to the archonship of Aristophanes (331/330) and Darius's death to that of Aristophon (330/329). This is the historical background against which 8:5–7 and 8:21 are read; it is not itself an identification of the symbols.

- *Supporting (direct):* Arbela fought in the archonship of Aristophanes, month Pyanepsion; Darius III died of wounds before Alexander saw him, archonship of Aristophon. (3.15; 3.21–22) [6]

### After Alexander, four of his successors (Cassander, Lysimachus, Ptolemy, Seleucus) acted as kings in alliance against Antigonus.

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Diodorus describes the four-king coalition before Ipsus. Jerome lists a different four, so the "four kingdoms" of 8:22 are matched to different sets by different interpreters.

- *Supporting (direct):* Cassander summoned Lysimachus; Ptolemy and Seleucus agreed to join them against Antigonus. (20.106.2–5) [7]
- *Context (indirect):* Jerome's four successors are Ptolemy, Philip Arrhidaeus, Seleucus and Antigonus. (on 8:8, 22) [8]

### Daniel was physically at Susa when he saw the vision.

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

Guzik reads 8:27 ("the king's business") as Daniel being in Shushan on official business; Driver reads 8:2 as describing where Daniel saw himself in the vision. In Belshazzar's time Susa lay outside Babylonian rule, which bears on the question but was not researched further.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Daniel "was in Shushan on business for the king". (on 8:2, 27) [5]
- *Challenging (indirect):* The verse describes where Daniel "seemed to find himself in the vision". (p. 111 (on 8:2)) [1]

### Alexander was shown the Book of Daniel at Jerusalem.

**Classification:** No independent corroboration found (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Reported only by Josephus. Arrian's narrative of the campaign from Tyre to Gaza and Egypt does not mention Jerusalem.

- *Supporting (direct):* Alexander was shown the Book of Daniel and supposed he was the Greek who would destroy the Persian empire. (Ant. 11.8.5) [9]
- *Context (direct):* Arbela fought in the archonship of Aristophanes, month Pyanepsion; Darius III died of wounds before Alexander saw him, archonship of Aristophon. (3.15; 3.21–22) [6]

*Limitations:* Absence in Arrian is not disproof.

### Gabriel explained the vision to Daniel.

**Classification:** Not empirically testable (machine proposed) · layer: text

An angelic revelation cannot be assessed historically. This is not a theological verdict.

- pro_01M4TTS0HJ5D1K16KS9EDABHHY → **direct reference** → Macedonian empire of Alexander the Great (high): The text names "Greece" (Yavan, 8:21); recorded against the Macedonian empire as the Greek power of the period.

## Commentary (interpretation, not historical evidence)

- Guzik reads the ram as Medo-Persia, the goat as Greece under Alexander and the four horns as his generals, and the little horn as Antiochus IV in a near fulfillment and the Antichrist in a far one; he prefers 2,300 literal days ending with the cleansing of the Temple and rejects William Miller's year-day reckoning. [5]

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- The Ulai's course at Susa not located.
- Old Greek Daniel 8 not read.
- Modern studies of Alexander at Jerusalem not consulted.
- Locate the Ulai precisely (Karkheh, Ab-i Diz or a canal).
- Old Greek variant at 8:14 not read.

## Disputes

- Daniel was physically at Susa when he saw the vision.

# Rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabaeus (25 Chislev 148 SE, 165/164 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- John 10:22 (reference): The Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem, commemorating this event.

## Biblical account

John mentions the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem in winter, the festival commemorating this rededication.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Seleucid rule over Judaea; reign of Antiochus IV (175–164 BC)

Antiochus IV's measures culminated in the "abomination of desolation" on the altar on 15 Chislev 145 SE (1 Macc 1:54). Three years later, on 25 Chislev 148, Judas Maccabaeus's party dedicated a new altar and instituted an eight-day festival (1 Macc 4:52–59), which Josephus says was called "Lights". The Babylonian King List reports Antiochus's death in Kislîmu 148 (Babylonian reckoning). [1, 2, 3]

- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: Seleucid king who suppressed Temple worship [1]

## Competing reconstructions

- **December 165 BC** (S. R. Driver (1900), J. A. Montgomery (1927), D. Guzik): Seleucid era counted from autumn 312 BC. [4, 5, 6]
- **December 164 BC** (Implied by Josephus's 154th Olympiad (operator calculation); many modern works (not verified directly)): Seleucid era counted from spring 311 BC. [2]

## Claims and evidence

### The Temple altar was rededicated on 25 Chislev 148 SE, three years after its desecration, and an eight-day festival was instituted.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

1 Maccabees gives the date and the festival; Josephus gives the same Seleucid years with Olympiad equivalents (he likely depends on 1 Maccabees for the narrative); John 10:22 independently attests that the Feast of the Dedication was kept in the first century.

- *Supporting (direct):* Desecration 15 Chislev 145; rededication 25 Chislev 148 "at the time and day the Gentiles had profaned it". (1 Macc 1:54; 4:52–54) [1]
- *Supporting (direct):* Desolation 145 SE (153rd Olympiad), rededication 25 Apellaeus 148 SE (154th Olympiad); festival called "Lights". (Ant. 12.7.6–7) [2]
- *Supporting (indirect):* Interval of 3 years and 10 days between the heathen altar and the new altar. (p. 119) [4]

*Limitations:* Josephus partly dependent on 1 Maccabees.

### The rededication took place in December 164 BC (rather than 165 BC).

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

Driver and Montgomery date it to Dec 165 on a Macedonian (autumn 312) Seleucid epoch; Josephus's 154th Olympiad points to 164/163 (operator calculation). The chronology window spans both.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Rededication in the 154th Olympiad, i.e. from summer 164 BC on the standard Olympiad epoch (operator calculation). (Ant. 12.7.6) [2]
- *Challenging (indirect):* Chislev Era Sel. 148 = December 165; profanation Chislev 145 = 168. (on 8:14 and 12:11) [5]
- *Context (indirect):* The era was reckoned in a Babylonian (spring, Nisannu) and a Macedonian (autumn) calendar; year 1 SE = 312/311 BCE. Does not say which 1 Maccabees uses. (Seleucid Era) [7]
- *Context (direct):* Cleansing on 25 Chislev; letters dated year 148 (Dioscorinthius, Xanthicus). (2 Macc 10:5; 11:21, 33, 38) [8]

*Limitations:* No modern study of the epochs read directly.

## Related passages and events

- this event → **source attestation** → John 10:22 (high): The Feast of the Dedication commemorating the rededication.

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- No accessible study states which Seleucid-era epoch 1 Maccabees uses; the question remains open (Iranica read; specialist literature not accessible).
- Read 2 Maccabees 10 and a modern treatment of the Seleucid-era epochs in 1 Maccabees.

## Disputes

- The rededication took place in December 164 BC (rather than 165 BC).

# Artaxerxes sends Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem, Nisan of his twentieth year (Neh 2:1–8)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Nehemiah 2:1–8 (narration)
- Nehemiah 1:1 (reference): Chislev "in the twentieth year" precedes Nisan of the twentieth year.

## Biblical account

Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, sad at news of Jerusalem's broken wall, asks Artaxerxes in Nisan of his twentieth year to send him to build the city of his fathers' tombs; the king grants letters to the governors beyond the River and to the keeper of the king's forest for timber for the citadel gates, the city wall and a house.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Achaemenid Persian rule over Judah

On Babylonian reckoning Artaxerxes I's twentieth year began 1 Nisan = 13 Apr 445. Anderson instead dates 1 Nisan 445 to 14 March from an astronomical new moon of 13 March. [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Artaxerxes I (Longimanus): Issuer [1]

Babylonian tablets and the Syene papyrus fix Artaxerxes I's accession in 465/464 and his reign to 424/423; year 20 began 1 Nisan 445. Whether Nehemiah counted the same way is a separate question (see competing reconstructions).

- *Supporting (direct):* Accession year attested 3 Jan 464 (Cowley 6); year 20 begins 13 Apr 445. (pp. 15–16; table) [1]

# Cyrus's proclamation permitting the return and the rebuilding of the Temple (Ezra 1; 6:3–5)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Ezra 1:1–4 (narration)
- 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 (parallel_account)
- Ezra 6:3–5 (reference): The Ecbatana memorandum.

## Biblical account

Cyrus, stirred by the LORD to fulfil Jeremiah's word, proclaims in writing throughout his kingdom that the God of heaven has charged him to build a house at Jerusalem, and that any of his people may go up and build it, helped by their neighbours' gifts.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Achaemenid Persian rule over Judah

The Cyrus Cylinder (Babylon, c. 539–530) records that Cyrus returned the images of gods to their sanctuaries and gathered and returned their inhabitants for cities across the Tigris and in Sumer and Akkad; it does not name Judah or Jerusalem. [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Cyrus II (the Great): Issuer [2]

## Competing reconstructions

- **538 BC (Cyrus's first Babylonian year)** (D. Guzik, S. R. Driver (edict of Cyrus, 538)): Year 1 = 24 Mar 538 – Mar 537 on Nisan reckoning. [4, 5, 2]

## Claims and evidence

### Cyrus permitted deported peoples to return and restored their sanctuaries, as Ezra 1 describes for Judah.

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

The Cyrus Cylinder states that Cyrus returned the gods to their places and gathered and returned the inhabitants of a list of cities in Mesopotamia and beyond the Tigris. This shows a policy consistent with Ezra 1, but the Cylinder does not mention Judah or Jerusalem, so it does not corroborate the Judean decree itself.

- *Supporting (indirect):* "I returned the images of the gods … to their places"; "I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings" — for Babylonian and trans-Tigridian cities; Judah not named. (Lines 30–33) [1]
- *Context (contextual):* Cyrus's first Babylonian year began 1 Nisan = 24 Mar 538. (p. 14 and table) [2]

*Limitations:* The Cylinder's list is regional (Mesopotamia and east of the Tigris).

- this event → **same event** → 2 Chronicles 36:22–23 (high): Parallel wording of the proclamation.
- this event → **followed by** → Darius I confirms Cyrus's decree and orders the Temple completed (Ezra 6:1–12) (high): Darius finds and confirms Cyrus's memorandum (Ezra 6:1–12).

# Darius I confirms Cyrus's decree and orders the Temple completed (Ezra 6:1–12)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Ezra 6:1–12 (narration)

## Biblical account

Darius orders the archives searched; a scroll found at Achmetha in Media records Cyrus's first-year decree for the Temple; Darius orders the governor not to hinder the work and to pay its costs from royal revenue.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Achaemenid Persian rule over Judah

Darius I became king in 522 after killing Bardiya (Behistun) and was recognised in Babylonia from early 521. Haggai and Zechariah date their prophecies about the rebuilding to his second year (Hag 1:1; Zech 1:1). [1]

- Darius I (the Great): Issuer [1]

### Darius I reigned from 522/521 to 486 BC, so his second and sixth years fall in 520/519 and 516/515.

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Babylonian contracts dated by Darius from early 521 to late 486, with a gap during the revolts, fix his regnal years.

- *Supporting (direct):* Darius I recognised in Babylonia from Feb 521 (possibly Dec 522); died Nov 486; year 1 began Nisan 521. (pp. 12–15; table) [1]

*Limitations:* The decree itself is attested only in Ezra.

Gabriel "whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning" (9:21; 8:16).
Montgomery equates the half-week with the 2,300 evenings and mornings (1,150 days); Clement (per Jerome) added the 2,300 days to the 490 years.
In the Maccabean reading the one who stops the sacrifice is the same king as the little horn of ch. 8.
Jesus cites "the abomination of desolation, spoken of through Daniel the prophet".
The continual burnt offering removed and "the abomination that makes desolate" set up.
Seven sabbaths of years (49) — the jubilee pattern behind "seven weeks" (Newton).
Gabriel reappears in Luke 1:19, 26.

# Gabriel comes at the evening offering with the word of the seventy weeks (Dan 9:20–27)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed

## Biblical references

- Daniel 9:20–23 (narration)

## Biblical account

While Daniel is still praying, Gabriel comes in swift flight about the time of the evening offering, says that a word went out at the beginning of Daniel's supplications because he is greatly loved, and gives him the word of the seventy weeks (recorded separately as a prophecy).

## Historical setting

**Period:** As the prayer (same day)

claims.statement: Onias III, the legitimate high priest, was murdered near Antioch at the instigation of Menelaus (c. 171 BC).
claims.reasoning: 2 Maccabees narrates the murder at Daphne; Driver reports that historians generally accept it (Ewald, Schürer, Graetz). But 2 Maccabees alone records it, and Josephus elsewhere (B.J.) has Onias flee to Egypt and found the Leontopolis temple; Wellhausen rejected the 2 Maccabees account (as reported by Driver). The identification of Onias with the "anointed one" of 9:26 is a separate, interpretive question.
limitations: Whether Josephus's Onias in B.J. 1.1.1 is Onias III or his son (as in Ant. 12.9.7) is itself disputed.

claims.statement: 1 Nisan of Artaxerxes I's twentieth year fell on 14 March 445 BC.
claims.reasoning: Anderson derives 14 March from the astronomical new moon of 13 March 445 BC computed for him at Greenwich, assuming no intercalary month. Parker & Dubberstein's Babylonian table (built from attested and reconstructed intercalations) places 1 Nisan of year 19 on 26 Mar 446 and of year 20 on 13 Apr 445 — 384 days apart, i.e. a thirteen-month year with an intercalary month (operator arithmetic from the table; whether that intercalation is attested or reconstructed was not checked in the plate). The Judean calendar of Nehemiah's day need not have intercalated as Babylon did, so the table does not prove Anderson wrong, but his date is not the Babylonian one. Separately, the 173,880-day interval: in the proleptic Julian calendar 14 Mar 445 BC to 6 Apr AD 32 is 173,882 days (Julian day numbers; operator calculation); Anderson reaches 173,880 by counting the end-days inclusively and adding only 116 leap days, applying the Gregorian three-in-four-centuries correction to Julian dates (his own footnote).
limitations: Judean vs Babylonian intercalation not established for 446/445.
P&D Plate I (attested vs reconstructed intercalations) not read in the OCR.

# Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years and prays (Dan 9:1–19)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 9:1–2 (superscription): First year of Darius son of Ahasuerus.
- Daniel 9:3–19 (narration): The prayer.

## Biblical account

In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, a Mede made king over the Chaldean realm, Daniel learns from the books that Jeremiah's word allotted seventy years to Jerusalem's desolations. He seeks God with fasting, sackcloth and ashes, confesses that Israel has sinned and that the curse written in the law of Moses has justly come upon it, and pleads for mercy on the desolate sanctuary and the city called by God's name.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Narrative setting: the first year after Babylon's fall to the Persians (539/538 BC on the text's own sequence); composition date disputed

Daniel dates the prayer by Darius the Mede, whom no external source names (see the Daniel 5–6 records and their open review). Babylon fell to Cyrus's army in October 539; Cyrus's first Babylonian year began 24 March 538. The prayer's concern — the end of seventy years and the desolate Temple — matches the period before the return. [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Darius the Mede: "Made king over the realm of the Chaldeans" (identity disputed)
- Cyrus II (the Great): King of Babylon and the lands from Oct 539 [1]

- **Darius the Mede as a literary conflation (critical view)** (S. R. Driver (1900)): If the author confused the Persian Darius with a Median ruler, the "first year" is a narrative date only. [2]

## Claims and evidence

### Onias III, the legitimate high priest, was murdered near Antioch at the instigation of Menelaus (c. 171 BC).

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: evidence

2 Maccabees narrates the murder at Daphne; Driver reports that historians generally accept it (Ewald, Schürer, Graetz). But 2 Maccabees alone records it, and Josephus elsewhere (B.J.) has Onias flee to Egypt and found the Leontopolis temple; Wellhausen rejected the 2 Maccabees account (as reported by Driver). The identification of Onias with the "anointed one" of 9:26 is a separate, interpretive question.

- *Supporting (direct):* Onias, in sanctuary at Daphne near Antioch, is lured out and killed by Andronicus at Menelaus's request; the king later executes Andronicus. (2 Macc 4:33–38) [6]
- *Supporting (indirect):* The account "is accepted generally by historians" (Ewald, Schürer, Graetz). (p. 140 n. 1) [2]
- *Challenging (indirect):* 2 Maccabees alone records it; Josephus (B.J. 1.1.1; 7.10.2–3) has Onias himself flee to Egypt and found the temple at Leontopolis; Wellhausen rejected the account. (p. 140 n. 1) [2]
- *Challenging (direct):* "Onias, the high priest, fled to Ptolemy" and built a temple in the nome of Heliopolis — a different end for the high priest named Onias. (B.J. 1.1.1) [7]

*Limitations:* Whether Josephus's Onias in B.J. 1.1.1 is Onias III or his son (as in Ant. 12.9.7) is itself disputed.

### 1 Nisan of Artaxerxes I's twentieth year fell on 14 March 445 BC.

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

Anderson derives 14 March from the astronomical new moon of 13 March 445 BC computed for him at Greenwich, assuming no intercalary month. Parker & Dubberstein's Babylonian table (built from attested and reconstructed intercalations) places 1 Nisan of year 19 on 26 Mar 446 and of year 20 on 13 Apr 445 — 384 days apart, i.e. a thirteen-month year with an intercalary month (operator arithmetic from the table; whether that intercalation is attested or reconstructed was not checked in the plate). The Judean calendar of Nehemiah's day need not have intercalated as Babylon did, so the table does not prove Anderson wrong, but his date is not the Babylonian one. Separately, the 173,880-day interval: in the proleptic Julian calendar 14 Mar 445 BC to 6 Apr AD 32 is 173,882 days (Julian day numbers; operator calculation); Anderson reaches 173,880 by counting the end-days inclusively and adding only 116 leap days, applying the Gregorian three-in-four-centuries correction to Julian dates (his own footnote).

- *Supporting (direct):* New moon 13 March 445 BC at 7h 9m (Jerusalem), from Airy's letter of 26 June 1877; "the 1st Nisan may be assigned to the 14th March". (pp. 123–124 and note) [8]
- *Challenging (direct):* 1 Nisan of year 20 = 13 April 445 BC in the Babylonian calendar. (Table, Artaxerxes I year 20) [1]
- *Context (direct):* 476 years × 365 + 24 days (inclusive) + 116 leap days = 173,880; the note explains the Gregorian correction of three leap years in four centuries. (p. 128 and note) [8]

*Limitations:* Judean vs Babylonian intercalation not established for 446/445. P&D Plate I (attested vs reconstructed intercalations) not read in the OCR.

### Gabriel brought Daniel the word of the seventy weeks.

**Classification:** Not empirically testable (machine proposed) · layer: text

An angelic revelation cannot be assessed historically. This is not a theological verdict.


### Ancient Jewish and Christian chronographers overestimated the length of the Persian period.

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Driver and Montgomery (after Schürer) cite Demetrius and Josephus as overestimating the interval from the exile to the Hellenistic period by decades — the basis on which critical scholars explain the 67-year excess in a Maccabean reading. Demetrius's figures are textually uncertain (Behrmann, as reported by Driver), and the primary texts were not read here.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Josephus reckons 639 years from Cyrus's second year to AD 70 and other overestimates; Demetrius reckons 573 years from the fall of Samaria to Ptolemy IV — about 73 too many. (p. 147) [2]

*Limitations:* Demetrius and Josephus not read directly on this point.

- this event → **direct reference** → The word to Jeremiah dated by Jeremiah 25:1 (high): The seventy-year word was given in Jehoiakim's fourth year (Jer 25:1, 11).

- this event → **thematic parallel** → Deuteronomy 28:15–68 (high): "The curse and the oath written in the law of Moses" (9:11).
- this event → **preceded by** → Belshazzar slain; Darius the Mede receives the kingdom (Dan 5:30–31) (high): Darius had been made king over the Chaldeans (9:1; 5:31).

## Commentary (interpretation, not historical evidence)

- Guzik leaves Darius unidentified, reads Jeremiah's seventy years literally from the first deportation in 605, and presents the prayer as a model of confession that takes God's promises as a reason to pray. [9]

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- Scofield Reference Bible (1917) notes on Daniel 9 not found online in the 1917 series.
- Hoehner (1977) not accessible.
- Old Greek and Theodotion of 9:24–27 not read (only as quoted by Driver).
- Qumran use of the seventy weeks (e.g. 11QMelchizedek) not researched.
- The patronymic "son of Ahasuerus" is unexplained by external sources.
- The relation of the prayer to Neh 9 and Baruch 1–2 was not researched.

## Disputes

- Onias III, the legitimate high priest, was murdered near Antioch at the instigation of Menelaus (c. 171 BC).
- 1 Nisan of Artaxerxes I's twentieth year fell on 14 March 445 BC.

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed

## Biblical account

Artaxerxes' letter authorises Ezra, priest and scribe, to go up with any Israelites who wish, to carry silver and gold for the Temple, to draw on the provincial treasury, and to appoint magistrates and judges who know the law of God.

## Historical setting

- *Context (indirect):* Ezra's seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus = Ol. 80.3, Julian Period 4257; mentions Funccius placing Ezra under Artaxerxes Mnemon. (ch. 10) [3]

*Limitations:* Identity of Artaxerxes not independently established.

## Related passages and events

- this event → **followed by** → Artaxerxes sends Nehemiah to rebuild Jerusalem, Nisan of his twentieth year (Neh 2:1–8) (medium): Nehemiah's mission follows in the same king's 20th year (if both are Artaxerxes I).

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- Modern Ezra–Nehemiah chronology not read.
- The Ezra–Nehemiah order (Artaxerxes I or II for Ezra) not researched from modern studies.

claims.statement: "King of Persia" was not a title borne by the Persian kings while their empire lasted, so its use in Dan 10:1 reflects a later writer.
claims.reasoning: Driver argues the title was given to Persian kings only after the empire, to distinguish them from Greek rulers. The Behistun inscription (§1, Livius translation) has Darius call himself "the king of Persia" among his titles (other renderings: "king in Persia"). The Hebrew usage in Ezra and Daniel versus royal Persian titulary is not settled by these two sources. Re-checked: the Old Persian of DB §1 reads xšâyathiya Pârsaiy (Livius transliteration). Pârsaiy is the locative ("king in Persia", operator note on standard Old Persian grammar), which Livius renders "of Persia"; so Darius used a Persia-title, but in the locative form, which narrows rather than removes the challenge to Driver's argument. Driver's point concerns the Hebrew/Aramaic usage "king of Persia" as a distinguishing title; Ezra–Nehemiah use it too.
limitations: Driver's claim is about Hebrew usage, Behistun about Persian titulary; neither source addresses the other directly.

# Daniel's vision by the Tigris in the third year of Cyrus (Dan 10:1–11:1)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 10:1 (superscription): Third year of Cyrus king of Persia.
- Daniel 10:2–21 (narration)
- Daniel 11:1 (narration): End of the speech.
- Daniel 11:2–45 (narration): The revelation spoken in the vision; its content is recorded as prophecy records.
- Daniel 12:1–4 (narration): End of the revelation (recorded as prophecy records).

## Biblical account

In Cyrus's third year Daniel mourns three weeks; on the 24th of the first month, by the Tigris, he sees a dazzling man in linen whom his companions do not see. He falls senseless, is raised by a hand, and told that his prayer was heard from the first day but the prince of Persia withstood the messenger 21 days until Michael helped. Strengthened again, he is told that the messenger will return to fight the prince of Persia, that the prince of Greece will come, and that he will reveal what is written in the writing of truth.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Early Persian rule in Babylonia: Cyrus's third Babylonian year (spring 536 – spring 535)

Two years after Cyrus's first-year decree (Ezra 1), Daniel is still in Babylonia. The 24th of the first month (Nisan) falls just after Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread (14–21 Nisan), which on Driver's reading lay within his three weeks of mourning. Hiddekel is the Tigris (Gen 2:14). [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Cyrus II (the Great): King ("third year of Cyrus king of Persia") [1]

- **An unnamed high angel** (Jephet, Calvin, Zöckler (reported by Montgomery), D. Guzik (leaning)): A third angel besides Gabriel and Michael; Guzik reasons that the figure needed Michael's help. [4, 5]
- **A Christophany (the pre-incarnate Son)** (Hippolytus and Ephrem (reported by Montgomery), "Some" (reported by Guzik)): The description is echoed in Rev 1:13–15 of the risen Jesus. [4, 5]
- **No conflict with Dan 1:21** (Jerome): Daniel "continued" in his high position until Cyrus's first year (1:21) but lived on; the vision in Cyrus's third year is not excluded. [6]

## Claims and evidence

### "King of Persia" was not a title borne by the Persian kings while their empire lasted, so its use in Dan 10:1 reflects a later writer.

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

Driver argues the title was given to Persian kings only after the empire, to distinguish them from Greek rulers. The Behistun inscription (§1, Livius translation) has Darius call himself "the king of Persia" among his titles (other renderings: "king in Persia"). The Hebrew usage in Ezra and Daniel versus royal Persian titulary is not settled by these two sources. Re-checked: the Old Persian of DB §1 reads xšâyathiya Pârsaiy (Livius transliteration). Pârsaiy is the locative ("king in Persia", operator note on standard Old Persian grammar), which Livius renders "of Persia"; so Darius used a Persia-title, but in the locative form, which narrows rather than removes the challenge to Driver's argument. Driver's point concerns the Hebrew/Aramaic usage "king of Persia" as a distinguishing title; Ezra–Nehemiah use it too.

- *Supporting (indirect):* "King of Persia": a title not borne by the Persian kings while the empire lasted, though often given them afterwards. (p. 152 (on 10:1)) [2]
- *Challenging (direct):* Darius: "the great king, king of kings, the king of Persia, the king of countries" (Livius translation). (DB §1) [7]
- *Context (direct):* xšâyathiya Pârsaiy — "king in/of Persia" (Livius renders "of"). (DB col. i line 2 (transliteration)) [7]

*Limitations:* Driver's claim is about Hebrew usage, Behistun about Persian titulary; neither source addresses the other directly.

### Daniel saw a heavenly messenger and heard of conflicts among heavenly princes.

**Classification:** Not empirically testable (machine proposed) · layer: text

Visionary and angelic experience cannot be assessed historically. This is not a theological verdict.


### The vision's date (24th of the first month, Cyrus's third year) fell just after Passover and Unleavened Bread, around April 536 BC.

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: reconstruction

Driver identifies the first month as Nisan, so the festivals of 14–21 Nisan fell within the three weeks; Parker & Dubberstein's table gives 1 Nisan of Cyrus's year 3 as 30 Mar 536, so the 24th ≈ 22 Apr 536 (operator arithmetic, Babylonian calendar).

- *Supporting (direct):* 1 Nisan of Cyrus's year 3 = 30 Mar 536 BC. (Cyrus table, year 3) [1]

*Limitations:* Assumes Babylonian Nisan reckoning for both the year and the month.

## Commentary (interpretation, not historical evidence)

- Guzik notes that Daniel, about 84, stayed in Babylon after the first return, reads the three weeks as a partial fast, takes the prince of Persia as a high-ranking demon resisting the answer to prayer, and leans toward identifying the man in linen as an angel rather than Christ. [5]

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- Deut 32:8 at Qumran not read directly.
- Old Greek of Daniel 10 not read.
- Old Greek and Theodotion differences in ch. 10 not read beyond Jerome's notes.
- Deut 32:8 in 4QDeut(j) ("sons of God") not read directly.

## Disputes

- "King of Persia" was not a title borne by the Persian kings while their empire lasted, so its use in Dan 10:1 reflects a later writer.

# Popillius Laenas orders Antiochus IV out of Egypt at Eleusis (168 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:29–30 (reference): Proposed correlation only.

## Biblical account

He returns to the south, but the latter time is not as the former, for ships of Kittim come against him; he is grieved and returns in indignation against the holy covenant.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Sixth Syrian War (170–168 BC)

Antiochus IV invaded Egypt in 170/169 and again in 168. Near Alexandria, at Eleusis, the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas handed him the Senate's decree, drew a circle round him and demanded an answer before he stepped out; Antiochus agreed to withdraw (Polybius 29.27). Driver: Kittim (Cyprus/western coastlands) here stands for the Roman envoys. [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: Seleucid king [1]
- Gaius Popillius Laenas: Roman envoy [1]
- Ptolemy VI Philometor: Ptolemaic king [2]

## Claims and evidence

### The Roman envoy Popillius Laenas compelled Antiochus IV to withdraw from Egypt by drawing a circle round him.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Polybius (a contemporary) and Livy (read directly; Livy draws on Polybius for eastern affairs, so the two are not fully independent) agree on the circle and the withdrawal; Jerome's version agrees in substance. Jerome calls the envoy "Marcus"; Driver gives "C. Popillius"; Livy here names only "Popilius" (several Popilii appear in books 44–45).

- *Supporting (direct):* Popilius drew a circle round Antiochus; after brief hesitation he said he would do all the Romans demanded. (29.27.5–6) [1]
- *Supporting (indirect):* Laenas drew a circle in the sand around Antiochus, who withdrew. (on 11:29–30) [3]
- *Supporting (direct):* The Roman envoys met Antiochus at Eleusine, four miles from Alexandria; Popilius drew a line round him with a wand; he replied he would do as the senate directed. (Livy 45.12) [4]
- *Context (indirect):* Eleusis, four miles from Alexandria; Livy 45.12. (p. 181) [2]

claims.reasoning: 2 Maccabees narrates his death (ch. 9) before the cleansing (10:1–8) and closes the section "such were the events of the end of Antiochus" (10:9); its letters of year 148 include one in which Antiochus V speaks of his father as dead (11:23). 1 Maccabees (6:1–16) and Josephus (Ant. 12.9.1) have him die in Persia after hearing that the Jews had pulled down the abomination. The Babylonian king list reports news of his death in Kislimu 148 SE (Babylonian reckoning) — the same month-name as the rededication (25 Chislev 148): if 1 Maccabees used the spring (Babylonian) epoch the two events fall within weeks of each other (Dec 164); on the autumn epoch the rededication (Dec 165) precedes the death by a year. 2 Maccabees' arrangement is often thought thematic, but that was not verified here. Unresolved.

# Death of Antiochus IV at Tabae in Persia (164 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:45 (reference): Proposed correlation only; the setting "between the sea and the glorious holy mountain" does not match Tabae.

## Biblical account

He plants the tents of his palace between the sea and the glorious holy mountain; yet he comes to his end, and no one helps him.

## Historical setting

**Period:** End of Antiochus IV's reign (164 BC)

Antiochus went east in 166/165 to raise funds; after failing to plunder a sanctuary of Artemis in Elymaïs he died at Tabae in Persia, "smitten with madness, as some say" (Polybius 31.9). News reached Babylon in Kislimu 148 SE (BM 35603). 1 Macc 6 adds that he heard of the Jews' victories; 2 Macc 9 tells the story with legendary additions (Driver). [1, 2, 3, 4]

### Rulers

- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: Seleucid king [2]

## Competing reconstructions

- **Death after the rededication** (1 Maccabees 6:7 (he hears that the abomination has been pulled down), Josephus, Ant. 12.9.1): Death in Persia after news of the Temple's recovery. [3, 5]
- **Death before the rededication** (2 Maccabees 9–10 (narrative order; read directly), 2 Macc 11:23 (Antiochus V's letter)): The death (ch. 9) precedes the cleansing (10:1–8); a letter of year 148 refers to the late king. Not modelled as a constraint because the sources disagree (claim under review). [6, 4]

## Claims and evidence

### Antiochus IV died at Tabae in Persia in 164 BC after a failed attempt to plunder a temple in Elymaïs.

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

A Greek historian, the Babylonian king list and 1 Maccabees agree.

- *Supporting (direct):* Thwarted at the sanctuary of Artemis in Elymaïs; died at Tabae in Persia. (31.9) [1]
- *Supporting (direct):* It was heard that Antiochus IV died. (rev., year 148 Kislimu) [2]
- *Supporting (direct):* Failed to take Elymaïs, fell sick and died in the 149th year (Macedonian epoch). (1 Macc 6:1–16) [3]
- *Supporting (direct):* Death in Persia; Josephus reports Polybius's explanation (the temple of Diana) and disputes it. (Ant. 12.9.1) [5]
- *Context (direct):* Places the failed temple robbery at Persepolis and the illness on the road from Ecbatana; he dies "in the mountains". (2 Macc 9:1–3, 28) [6]

### Daniel 11:40–45 accurately describes the circumstances of Antiochus IV's last campaign and death.

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

Porphyry's reconstruction (via Jerome) is the only source for a fourth Egyptian campaign; Driver judges it suspect. Futurist interpreters avoid the problem by referring 11:36–45 to a future figure. Recorded as disputed.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Porphyry claims a fourth Egyptian campaign, a march east against Artaxias, a camp at "Apedno" between Tigris and Euphrates, and death at Tabae. (on 11:40–45 (Porphyry)) [7]
- *Challenging (indirect):* No hint of a final conquest of Egypt outside Jerome; Egypt was under Roman protection; Antiochus was in financial difficulty; he died in Persia, not between the sea and the holy mountain. (pp. 196–197; Introduction p. xc) [4]
- *Challenging (direct):* Death at Tabae in Persia. (31.9) [1]

### Antiochus IV died before the Temple was rededicated.

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

2 Maccabees narrates his death (ch. 9) before the cleansing (10:1–8) and closes the section "such were the events of the end of Antiochus" (10:9); its letters of year 148 include one in which Antiochus V speaks of his father as dead (11:23). 1 Maccabees (6:1–16) and Josephus (Ant. 12.9.1) have him die in Persia after hearing that the Jews had pulled down the abomination. The Babylonian king list reports news of his death in Kislimu 148 SE (Babylonian reckoning) — the same month-name as the rededication (25 Chislev 148): if 1 Maccabees used the spring (Babylonian) epoch the two events fall within weeks of each other (Dec 164); on the autumn epoch the rededication (Dec 165) precedes the death by a year. 2 Maccabees' arrangement is often thought thematic, but that was not verified here. Unresolved.

- *Supporting (direct):* Death narrated before the cleansing; Antiochus V's letter refers to his father having passed to the gods. (2 Macc 9:1–29; 10:1–9; 11:23) [6]
- *Challenging (direct):* In Persia he hears that the Jews had pulled down the abomination, falls sick and dies. (1 Macc 6:5–16) [3]
- *Challenging (direct):* He dies in Persia after hearing of the Jews' success. (Ant. 12.9.1) [5]
- *Context (direct):* News of the death heard in Kislimu 148 SE (Babylonian reckoning). (rev., year 148 Kislimu) [2]

*Limitations:* Depends on the unresolved Seleucid-era epoch of 1 Maccabees. Modern studies of 2 Macc 11's letters not read.

- Daniel 11:40–45 accurately describes the circumstances of Antiochus IV's last campaign and death.

# Battle of Panium: Antiochus III defeats Scopas (c. 200–198 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:15–16 (reference): Proposed correlation only.

## Biblical account

The king of the north casts up a mound and takes a fortified city; the south cannot stand; he stands in the glorious land.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Fifth Syrian War (202–195 BC)

With Ptolemy V a child, Antiochus III invaded Coele-Syria; the Ptolemaic general Scopas was defeated near Paneion and later surrendered at Sidon; Judaea passed to Seleucid rule and Jerusalem received Antiochus (Polybius 16.39, quoted by Josephus). [1, 2, 3]

### Rulers

- Antiochus III the Great: Seleucid king [1]
- Ptolemy V Epiphanes: Ptolemaic king (a child) [3]

## Competing reconstructions

- **200 BC** (Common modern date (not verified directly)): Battle in 200, surrender of Sidon later.
- **198 BC** (S. R. Driver (1900)): "Defeated at Paneion in 198". [2]

## Claims and evidence

### Antiochus III defeated the Ptolemaic general Scopas at Panium and took control of Coele-Syria and Judaea.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Polybius (partly via Josephus) and Jerome agree; the exact year is uncertain in the sources read.

- *Supporting (direct):* Scopas despaired of victory and retreated; after Scopas was conquered Antiochus occupied Samaria, Abila and Gadara, and the Jews of Jerusalem submitted. (16.19.10; 16.39.3–4) [1]
- *Supporting (indirect):* Antiochus put Scopas to flight near the sources of the Jordan and besieged him in Sidon. (on 11:15–16) [3]
- *Supporting (direct):* Antiochus overcame Scopas at the fountains of Jordan; the Jews received him into Jerusalem; Josephus quotes Polybius book 16. (Ant. 12.3.3) [4]

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- Exact year (200 or 198) not fixed by the sources read.

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:18 (reference): Proposed correlation only.

## Biblical account

The king of the north turns to the coastlands and takes many, but a commander puts an end to his insolence.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Roman–Seleucid War (192–188 BC)

Antiochus III crossed into Greece, was defeated at Thermopylae (191) and then at Magnesia near Smyrna by Lucius Scipio (190); by the subsequent treaty he gave up Asia Minor west of the Taurus (Driver after Livy; Jerome). [1, 2, 3]

### Rulers

- Antiochus III the Great: Seleucid king (defeated) [1]
- Lucius Cornelius Scipio (Asiaticus): Roman commander [1]

## Claims and evidence

### Antiochus III was defeated by the Romans at Magnesia (190 BC) and forced to give up Asia Minor west of the Taurus.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Livy (read directly) and Jerome/Porphyry agree, with Appian's battle narrative as context. Livy's casualty figures are his own.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Decisive battle in autumn 190 at Magnesia; Antiochus's army defeated by Lucius Cornelius Scipio (Livy 37.39–44); renounced claims west of the Taurus. (pp. 175–176 (on 11:18)) [1]
- *Supporting (indirect):* Vanquished by Lucius Scipio with Africanus and confined beyond the Taurus. (on 11:17–19) [2]
- *Supporting (direct):* Antiochus encamped near Magnesia at Sipylus; his army was routed by the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio; up to 50,000 foot and 3,000 horse said to have been killed. (Livy 37.38–44) [4]
- *Context (contextual):* Battle narrative: the phalanx "broke into disorderly flight". (Syr. 34–35) [3]

# Battle of Raphia: Ptolemy IV defeats Antiochus III (217 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:11–12 (reference): Proposed correlation only (Jerome; Driver; Guzik); Daniel names no king or place.

## Biblical account

Daniel speaks of the king of the south, angered, defeating the great army of the king of the north but not prevailing. (The text names no one; the correlation is the interpreters'.)

## Historical setting

**Period:** Fourth Syrian War (219–217 BC)

Antiochus III had recovered much of Coele-Syria; Ptolemy IV met him near Raphia. Polybius describes Antiochus's wing succeeding while his left and phalanx broke; Antiochus withdrew with heavy losses, Ptolemy recovered Coele-Syria and agreed a one-year truce. [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Antiochus III the Great: Seleucid king (defeated) [1]
- Ptolemy IV Philopator: Ptolemaic king (victor) [1]

## Claims and evidence

### Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III at Raphia and recovered Coele-Syria, then granted a truce.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

Polybius is a near-contemporary historian; Jerome's account (from Porphyry and Greek historians) agrees. Both lines are literary; no inscription was read here.

- *Supporting (direct):* Antiochus withdrew to Raphia with about 10,000 foot lost; Ptolemy took Raphia and recovered Coele-Syria; a truce for a year. (5.85–87) [1]
- *Supporting (indirect):* Antiochus lost his army at Raphia and conceded Syria. (on 11:11–12) [3]

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- The Raphia decree (Pithom stele) not read.

# Desecration of the Temple: the "abomination of desolation" (15 Chislev 145 SE, 168/167 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `needs_review` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:31 (reference): Proposed correlation only.
- Matthew 24:15 (reference): Jesus refers to "the abomination of desolation, spoken of through Daniel".

## Biblical account

Forces from him profane the sanctuary, take away the continual burnt offering and set up the abomination that makes desolate. (Daniel names no king; 1 Maccabees narrates the event.)

## Historical setting

**Period:** Reign of Antiochus IV (175–164 BC)

After his return from Egypt Antiochus IV plundered the Temple (1 Macc 1:20–24, year 143); later a royal decree banned Jewish practice, and on 15 Chislev 145 an "abomination of desolation" was built on the altar, with pagan sacrifice from 25 Chislev (1 Macc 1:54, 59). Josephus dates it to 145 SE in the 153rd Olympiad. [1, 2, 3]

### Rulers

- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: Seleucid king [1]

*Computed ranges are reconstructions that depend on the named chronology model and the stated assumptions. They are not independent dates.*


**Chronological statements:**

- “After his return from Egypt … the king sent letters … that they should profane the sanctuary (1 Macc 1:20–54)” (Daniel 11:30–31) → `after` Popillius Laenas orders Antiochus IV out of Egypt at Eleusis (168 BC); assumptions: 1 Maccabees places the plunder of the Temple after the first Egyptian campaign (143 SE) and the desecration two years later; Jerome says the profanation came two years after the plunder. [1, 4]
- “at the time and on the day the Gentiles had profaned it, on that day it was dedicated (1 Macc 4:54)” (John 10:22) → `months_later` this event; assumptions: From 15 Chislev 145 to 25 Chislev 148: three years and ten days (Driver); 36–38 months allows for intercalary months. [1, 3]

## Competing reconstructions

- **December 168 BC** (J. A. Montgomery (1927), S. R. Driver (Macedonian epoch)): Seleucid era from autumn 312. [5, 3]
- **December 167 BC** (Spring-311 epoch (operator conversion; many modern works, not verified directly)): Seleucid era from spring 311. [1]

## Claims and evidence

### On 15 Chislev 145 SE an "abomination of desolation" was set up on the Temple altar and the regular offerings ceased.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

1 Maccabees and Josephus agree on the year and act (Josephus partly depends on 1 Maccabees).

- *Supporting (direct):* 15 Chislev 145: an abomination of desolation built on the altar; sacrifice on the idol altar from the 25th. (1 Macc 1:54–59) [1]
- *Supporting (direct):* Desolation in 145 SE, 153rd Olympiad; "according to the prophecy of Daniel". (Ant. 12.5.4; 12.7.6) [2]
- *Supporting (direct):* The sanctuary in Jerusalem was polluted and called by the name of Olympian Zeus. (2 Macc 6:2) [6]

*Limitations:* Josephus partly dependent on 1 Maccabees.

### The desecration took place in December 167 BC (rather than 168 BC).

**Classification:** Disputed (requires review) · layer: reconstruction

Same Seleucid-era epoch question as the rededication; the synchronism window spans both years.

- *Supporting (indirect):* 153rd Olympiad (168–164 BC) — consistent with either year (operator note). (Ant. 12.5.4) [2]
- *Challenging (indirect):* Profanation Chislev 145 = 168. (on 8:14 and 12:11) [5]
- *Context (indirect):* The era was reckoned in a Babylonian (spring, Nisannu) and a Macedonian (autumn) calendar; year 1 SE = 312/311 BCE. Does not say which 1 Maccabees uses. (Seleucid Era) [7]

## Related passages and events

- this event → **followed by** → Rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabaeus (25 Chislev 148 SE, 165/164 BC) (high): Three years and ten days later the altar was rededicated (1 Macc 4:52–54). [1]
- this event → **thematic parallel** → Matthew 24:15 (high): Jesus cites Daniel's "abomination of desolation" for a coming desolation.
- this event → **thematic parallel** → Mark 13:14 (medium): Mark's parallel to Matt 24:15: "the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet".

## Unanswered questions and research gaps

- No accessible study states which Seleucid-era epoch 1 Maccabees uses; the question remains open (Iranica read; specialist literature not accessible).

## Disputes

- The desecration took place in December 167 BC (rather than 168 BC).

claims.statement: The son of Antiochus III who succeeded him and was killed in 175 BC was Seleucus IV, not Seleucus III.
claims.reasoning: The Babylonian king list records Antiochus III's death in SE 125 and the accession of his son Seleucus (IV) for twelve years; Appian names Seleucus, killed through Heliodorus; Jerome calls the king of 11:20 "Seleucus surnamed Philopator, the son of Antiochus the Great". Seleucus III (Ceraunus) was Antiochus III's elder brother and predecessor (Jerome on 11:10). Guzik's naming of "Seleucus III" at 11:20 therefore appears to be a slip for Seleucus IV; it is recorded as a variant on the prophecy record, not corrected in his name.

Names "Seleucus III, the eldest son of Antiochus III".

# Assassination of Seleucus IV and accession of Antiochus IV (175 BC)

> **Status:** Researched — not human reviewed · research status `publishable` · revision 1 · last reviewed: not reviewed
> Programmatic validation is not historical verification. Classifications are machine-proposed unless marked as owner-reviewed.

## Biblical references

- Daniel 11:20–21 (reference): Proposed correlation only.

## Biblical account

One who sends an exactor through the glory of the kingdom is destroyed within a few days, not in anger or battle; in his place a contemptible person arises.

## Historical setting

**Period:** Seleucid dynasty, 175 BC

Seleucus IV, son of Antiochus III, reigned 12 years (BM 35603) and was killed in a conspiracy of Heliodorus (Appian, Syr. 45); Antiochus IV, his brother, was installed with the help of Eumenes and Attalus. The king list records Seleucus's death and Antiochus's accession in Ululu 137 SE. [1, 2]

### Rulers

- Seleucus IV Philopator: Seleucid king (killed) [1]
- Antiochus IV Epiphanes: Successor [1]

## Claims and evidence

### Seleucus IV was killed in a conspiracy led by Heliodorus in 175 BC, and Antiochus IV took the throne.

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

A Greek historian and a contemporary Babylonian king list agree on the succession; the king list dates it.

- *Supporting (direct):* Seleucus assassinated in a conspiracy of Heliodorus; Eumenes and Attalus installed Antiochus. (Syr. 45) [2]
- *Supporting (direct):* Seleucus IV died on 10 Ululu 137; the same month Antiochus IV ascended. (rev., year 137 Ululu) [1]

### The son of Antiochus III who succeeded him and was killed in 175 BC was Seleucus IV, not Seleucus III.

**Classification:** Independently corroborated (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

The Babylonian king list records Antiochus III's death in SE 125 and the accession of his son Seleucus (IV) for twelve years; Appian names Seleucus, killed through Heliodorus; Jerome calls the king of 11:20 "Seleucus surnamed Philopator, the son of Antiochus the Great". Seleucus III (Ceraunus) was Antiochus III's elder brother and predecessor (Jerome on 11:10). Guzik's naming of "Seleucus III" at 11:20 therefore appears to be a slip for Seleucus IV; it is recorded as a variant on the prophecy record, not corrected in his name.

- *Supporting (direct):* Antiochus III killed in Elam (125); his son Seleucus ascends, reigns 12 years; Seleucus dies 137. (rev., years 125 and 137) [1]
- *Supporting (direct):* Seleucus assassinated in Heliodorus's conspiracy; Antiochus installed by Eumenes and Attalus. (Syr. 45) [2]
- *Supporting (indirect):* Seleucus Ceraunus and Antiochus the Great were sons of Seleucus Callinicus; the king of 11:20 is Seleucus Philopator, son of Antiochus the Great. (on 11:10, 11:20) [3]
- *Supporting (indirect):* King Seleucus funded the sacrifices and sent his chancellor Heliodorus for the Temple treasury. (2 Macc 3:3, 7) [4]
- *Context (indirect):* Names "Seleucus III, the eldest son of Antiochus III". (on 11:20) [5]

event.title: The closing dialogue by the river: the oath, the numbers and Daniel's dismissal (Dan 12:5–13)
event.summary: At the end of the vision Daniel sees two figures on the river banks; the man in linen swears that the end will come after a time, times and a half; Daniel, not understanding, is told the words are sealed, given the 1,290 and 1,335 days, and dismissed to rest until he rises to his portion at the end of the days. This record is the narrated scene; the numbers and their interpretations are a separate prophecy record.

text_summary.body: Two figures stand on either bank; one asks the man in linen, who is above the waters, how long until the end of these wonders. Raising both hands to heaven he swears by the one who lives forever: a time, times and a half, when the shattering of the holy people's power is complete. Daniel asks the outcome and is told to go his way; the words are sealed; the wise will understand. From the removal of the continual offering and the abomination there will be 1,290 days; blessed is the one who reaches 1,335. Daniel will rest and stand in his lot at the end of the days.

setting.period: As the vision of ch. 10 (Cyrus's third year, 536/535 BC) on the text's own dating
setting.body: The scene returns to the river of 10:4; Jerome identifies the two figures as the angels of the Greeks and Persians and the man in linen as the angel who presented Daniel's prayers. The numbers take as their starting point the removal of the continual offering and the abomination of 11:31.

claims.statement: The Temple lay desecrated for three years and ten days (15 Chislev 145 – 25 Chislev 148), not three and a half years.
claims.reasoning: 1 Maccabees gives both dates (15 Chislev 145; 25 Chislev 148), and Josephus's Antiquities says three years. Three sources give round figures that differ: Josephus's Jewish War "three years and six months" (which Montgomery takes as an accommodation to Daniel) and 2 Maccabees "two years" (2 Macc 10:3, perhaps counting from a different starting point). The dated account of 1 Maccabees is preferred because it supplies both termini; the other figures are recorded as counterevidence.
limitations: 2 Maccabees' starting point for its "two years" is not stated.

claims.statement: 1,290 days counted from 15 Chislev 145 SE end about June 164 BC, close to the death of Antiochus IV.
claims.reasoning: Driver (after Cornill: 6 June 164) computes the end from a December 168 start; the death was reported in Babylon in Kislimu 148 (≈ Nov–Dec 164). The arithmetic is sound if the desecration is in 168; on a 167 start it would end in mid-163, after the death was known. Depends on a disputed epoch.
limitations: Depends on the 168/167 question (review open).

claims.statement: Daniel 12:2 is the first Old Testament text to teach a resurrection of the wicked as well as the righteous.
claims.reasoning: Driver traces national resurrection (Hos 6:2; Ezek 37) and individual resurrection limited to Israel (Isa 26:19) before Dan 12:2; Jerome reads 12:2 as the resurrection of all the dead. This is a claim about the history of ideas resting on one modern commentator, not on independent evidence.
limitations: Dating of Isa 24–27 and of Daniel affects the claim.

claims.statement: An angel swore the duration of the end; the dead will rise.
claims.reasoning: Visionary content and a future resurrection cannot be assessed historically. This is not a theological verdict.

evidence.finding: Desecration 15 Chislev 145; rededication 25 Chislev 148.
The Temple desolate three years; desolation 145, rededication 148.
Josephus B.J. 1.1.1 states the profanation lasted 3½ years — an accommodation to Daniel (Montgomery).
Terminus a quo 15 Chisleu 168; 1,290 days end in June (Cornill: 6 June) 164; Antiochus died in 164.
Porphyry already referred the 1,290 days to Antiochus's desolation.
"A resurrection of the wicked is taught for the first time"; "many" limits it to Israelites.
Resurrection of all the dead, "some unto eternal life and others unto eternal shame".
The daily sacrifice stopped "for three years and six months".
Sacrifices offered "after they had ceased for two years".

research_gaps: Qumran Daniel witnesses for ch. 12 not read.

name_searches.name: time, times and half a time

relationships.rationale: The end of the 1,290 days from the desecration coincides roughly with the death of Antiochus IV (164 BC).
The 1,335th day marks the cleansing of the Temple after victory over Antiochus's generals.
The "awakening" of 12:2 is the Maccabean loyalists' return to victory, read metaphorically.

The text's starting point — "the continual burnt offering taken away and the abomination that makes desolate set up" — repeats 11:31; preterist interpreters identify it with 15 Chislev 145 SE, futurists with a future event.
Another number for the period of the removed continual offering (2,300 evenings and mornings, 8:14).
"A time, times and half a time" (7:25; 12:7).
Half a week with the sacrifice made to cease (9:27) — linked by futurist and preterist readers alike.
1,260 days in Revelation (also 11:3; "time, times and half a time" in 12:14).
"Your dead shall live … awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust" (Driver).
Those in the tombs come out, to a resurrection of life or of judgment.
"Great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world" echoes 12:1.
The dead judged from what is written in the books (cf. "written in the book", 12:1).
Michael, "your prince" (10:21), now "the great prince who stands for the children of your people".
"At that time" ties 12:1 to the end of the wilful king (11:45).
Contrast: "Don't seal up the words of the prophecy of this book".
The same vision by the river (10:4; 12:5–6).

## Biblical account

Two figures stand on either bank; one asks the man in linen, who is above the waters, how long until the end of these wonders. Raising both hands to heaven he swears by the one who lives forever: a time, times and a half, when the shattering of the holy people's power is complete. Daniel asks the outcome and is told to go his way; the words are sealed; the wise will understand. From the removal of the continual offering and the abomination there will be 1,290 days; blessed is the one who reaches 1,335. Daniel will rest and stand in his lot at the end of the days.

## Historical setting

**Period:** As the vision of ch. 10 (Cyrus's third year, 536/535 BC) on the text's own dating

The scene returns to the river of 10:4; Jerome identifies the two figures as the angels of the Greeks and Persians and the man in linen as the angel who presented Daniel's prayers. The numbers take as their starting point the removal of the continual offering and the abomination of 11:31. [1]

## Claims and evidence

### The Temple lay desecrated for three years and ten days (15 Chislev 145 – 25 Chislev 148), not three and a half years.

**Classification:** Strongly supported (machine proposed) · layer: evidence

1 Maccabees gives both dates (15 Chislev 145; 25 Chislev 148), and Josephus's Antiquities says three years. Three sources give round figures that differ: Josephus's Jewish War "three years and six months" (which Montgomery takes as an accommodation to Daniel) and 2 Maccabees "two years" (2 Macc 10:3, perhaps counting from a different starting point). The dated account of 1 Maccabees is preferred because it supplies both termini; the other figures are recorded as counterevidence.

- *Supporting (direct):* Desecration 15 Chislev 145; rededication 25 Chislev 148. (1 Macc 1:54; 4:52–54) [4]
- *Supporting (direct):* The Temple desolate three years; desolation 145, rededication 148. (Ant. 12.7.6) [5]
- *Challenging (indirect):* Josephus B.J. 1.1.1 states the profanation lasted 3½ years — an accommodation to Daniel (Montgomery). (Introduction, p. 97 n.) [6]
- *Challenging (direct):* The daily sacrifice stopped "for three years and six months". (B.J. 1.1.1) [7]
- *Challenging (direct):* Sacrifices offered "after they had ceased for two years". (2 Macc 10:3) [8]

*Limitations:* 2 Maccabees' starting point for its "two years" is not stated.

### 1,290 days counted from 15 Chislev 145 SE end about June 164 BC, close to the death of Antiochus IV.

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: reconstruction

Driver (after Cornill: 6 June 164) computes the end from a December 168 start; the death was reported in Babylon in Kislimu 148 (≈ Nov–Dec 164). The arithmetic is sound if the desecration is in 168; on a 167 start it would end in mid-163, after the death was known. Depends on a disputed epoch.

- *Supporting (indirect):* Terminus a quo 15 Chisleu 168; 1,290 days end in June (Cornill: 6 June) 164; Antiochus died in 164. (p. 205 (on 12:11)) [9]
- *Context (indirect):* Porphyry already referred the 1,290 days to Antiochus's desolation. (on 12:11) [1]

*Limitations:* Depends on the 168/167 question (review open).

### Daniel 12:2 is the first Old Testament text to teach a resurrection of the wicked as well as the righteous.

**Classification:** Historically plausible (machine proposed) · layer: reconstruction

Driver traces national resurrection (Hos 6:2; Ezek 37) and individual resurrection limited to Israel (Isa 26:19) before Dan 12:2; Jerome reads 12:2 as the resurrection of all the dead. This is a claim about the history of ideas resting on one modern commentator, not on independent evidence.

- *Supporting (indirect):* "A resurrection of the wicked is taught for the first time"; "many" limits it to Israelites. (Introduction pp. xcii–xciii; p. 201) [9]
- *Context (indirect):* Resurrection of all the dead, "some unto eternal life and others unto eternal shame". (on 12:2, 13) [1]

*Limitations:* Dating of Isa 24–27 and of Daniel affects the claim.

### An angel swore the duration of the end; the dead will rise.

**Classification:** Not empirically testable (machine proposed) · layer: text

Visionary content and a future resurrection cannot be assessed historically. This is not a theological verdict.
